headline: Intuit: earnings up 56% on 12% revenue growth, and Mailchimp is being sold
takeaway: Revenue rose 12% to $4.4 billion and adjusted EPS of $2.91 beat the $2.64 consensus by 10%, as operating income grew four times faster than sales. Intuit also agreed to sell Mailchimp, the email-marketing business it bought in 2021, and trimmed its full-year revenue outlook because of a change at Credit Karma.
results: Intuit reported revenue of $4.4 billion for its fiscal first quarter ended October 31, up 12%. Adjusted earnings per share rose 56% to $2.91, against a consensus of about $2.64; reported EPS rose 63% to $2.59. Adjusted operating income grew 46% to $1.0 billion.

The Global Business Solutions segment — QuickBooks and the services around it — grew 15% to $3.1 billion, with online ecosystem revenue up 20% to $2.4 billion. QuickBooks Online Accounting revenue rose 19% on higher effective prices, mix and customer growth, and online services such as payments and payroll rose 21%.

Consumer revenue grew 7% to $958 million, with Credit Karma up 9% to $708 million; TurboTax is seasonally small in this quarter. Mailchimp revenue fell 1% to $313 million. Intuit repurchased $1.5 billion of stock, 73% more than a year earlier, and ended the quarter with $5.3 billion of cash and investments against $6.9 billion of debt.
mgmt: Chairman and chief executive Sasan Goodarzi called it a solid quarter with results above the top end of guidance, and said the company’s AI-driven platform is increasingly doing more of the work for consumers, businesses and accountants.

Chief financial officer Sandeep Aujla said the focus is on durable long-term revenue growth while expanding margins and increasing returns to shareholders. Intuit announced a definitive agreement to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons, expected to close in early 2027; guidance does not yet reflect the sale.

The company updated its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $23.08 billion to $23.37 billion, growth of 8% to 9%, citing a change at Credit Karma, which is now expected to grow 3% to 7%. It reiterated its operating income and EPS guidance for the year, and expects Global Business Solutions to grow 13% to 14%.
view: The Mailchimp sale is the most important line in this release, and it is an admission. Intuit paid about $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021, at the peak of software valuations, on the theory that small businesses would run their marketing and their books on one platform. Five years later the business is shrinking 1% while the rest of Intuit grows in the teens. Selling it is the right decision — a declining unit dilutes growth and distracts management — but investors should note what it says about the company’s record on large acquisitions, and expect a sale price far below the purchase price.

The core is as good as it has ever been. QuickBooks Online growing 19%, with payments and payroll growing 21%, describes a business with real pricing power over customers who rarely leave: an accountant’s software is embedded in how a small business runs. Operating income growing 46% on 12% revenue growth shows how much cost discipline has been applied — and how much the heavy investment of recent years is now being harvested. Margin expansion of this size cannot repeat every year, but it shows what the model can earn.

The soft spot is the consumer side. Credit Karma’s growth outlook was cut to 3% to 7%, and a business that earns referral fees from lenders is tied to credit conditions Intuit does not control. TurboTax is guided to grow only 2% to 3%, which reflects the ceiling on a product with a dominant share of a market that grows with the number of taxpayers. Total revenue growth of 8% to 9% is slower than Intuit’s history of low-to-mid teens, and that is why a stock once valued as a fast grower has been re-rated.

The long-term question is artificial intelligence, and it cuts both ways. Intuit’s pitch is that AI lets it do the bookkeeping and tax work for the customer and charge more for the outcome. The counter-argument is that general-purpose AI tools make tax preparation and basic bookkeeping easier to do without specialist software. The evidence so far favours Intuit — customers are paying higher prices, not leaving — but the shares fell sharply after the last two reports for a reason. With buybacks up 73%, management is signalling it thinks the market’s worry is overdone.
watch: The Mailchimp sale price and what Intuit does with the proceeds, and QuickBooks Online growth. The first shows how much value the acquisition destroyed; the second is the clearest test of whether AI is helping or eroding the core franchise.
